summary: Translation is a slide: every point of a shape moves the same amount left/right and up/down, with size, shape and orientation unchanged. On a first-quadrant coordinate grid, learners describe a move from one position to another ('3 units right'), carry out a two-part translation ('4 right and 2 up') and state new coordinates, and predict an image before plotting. The core procedural insight: a horizontal move changes only the x-coordinate (right adds to x), a vertical move only the y-coordinate (up adds to y). The main errors mirror coordinate errors — reversing the right/up amounts, changing the wrong coordinate, direction/sign slips, off-by-one line counting, and confusing the description of the move with the destination coordinates.
misconceptions: Reversal — swapping the right and up amounts (applying the horizontal shift to y and the vertical to x).
Changing the wrong coordinate — altering y for a move described as 'right', or changing both coordinates for a single-direction move.
Getting the direction sign wrong — moving left when 'right' is stated, or subtracting instead of adding.
Counting squares rather than numbered lines, giving an off-by-one image position.
Confusing the description of the MOVE with the destination coordinates (stating where it ends when asked how it moved, or vice versa).

activities.title: Predict-then-slide on a coordinate grid
steps: Set a translation such as '4 right and 2 up' on a first-quadrant grid containing a shape.
Before anything moves, predict and state (or type) the new coordinates of one named vertex — e.g. from (2,3) you should get (6,5).
Trigger the slide and watch every vertex glide by the same 4-across, 2-up while a coordinate readout ticks from the old to the new values.
Run a horizontal-only move (e.g. '3 right') and confirm the up-number (y) stays fixed while only the across-number changes.
Check two different vertices moved by identical amounts, confirming the shape did not turn, flip or resize.
Count the move in unit jumps from the start point, without counting the starting line itself as 'one'.
activities.insight: A horizontal move changes only x and a vertical move only y; the whole shape shifts uniformly without changing size or orientation, and predicting from the (x+right, y+up) rule can be checked against the actual slide.

activities.title: Describe the move between two positions
steps: Look at two marked positions on the grid, e.g. a start at (2,3) and an image at (5,3).
State the move in words — '3 units right' — using units and direction, not the destination coordinates.
For the same slide, separately answer 'where is it now?' with the end coordinates, so the two questions are practised side by side.
Describe the reverse move that returns the image to the start (e.g. (5,3) back to (2,3) is '3 units left'), surfacing reversibility.
activities.insight: Describing a move ('how did it move?' — units and direction) is a different answer from naming the destination ('where is it now?' — coordinates); learners must hold both apart.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal before-and-after picture (scaffold)
steps: Study a fixed picture showing a shape in its start position and its translated image with a slide arrow.
Tap the start and the image to reveal how the x- and y-coordinates changed between them.
Use a 'where does it land after 3 right?' flap to check a predicted position against the revealed answer.
activities.insight: A worked before-and-after slide shows how each coordinate changed and reinforces that the shape keeps its size and orientation.

checkQuestion: On a first-quadrant grid, mark a point at (2,3). Say: (1) 'Move a counter from (2,3) to (5,3) — describe that move in words.' (2) 'Now translate this shape 4 units right and 2 units up; plot it and write the new coordinates of this corner.' (3) 'A point is at (3,1). Without plotting, tell me where it lands after moving 2 right and 3 up.' Watch how they handle each — do not prompt the rule.
checkAnswer: (1) '3 units to the right' (only x changes, 2→5). (2) the corner moves from (2,3) to (6,5) — x + 4, y + 2 — and the whole shape slides by the same amount, same size and orientation. (3) (5,4) — predicts by adding 2 to x and 3 to y without needing to plot.
